old.adversarial-verification: Use when a consequential, surprising, high-stakes, novel, safety-relevant, research, proof, benchmark, or "verified" claim needs stronger checking than ordinary review, especially when one passing test or one evaluator could create false confidence.
old.check-the-work: Verify work that another agent, subagent, contractor or teammate reports as done, fixed, merged, deployed or live, using the primary record (git, CI, the running system) instead of their report. Use when accepting delegated work, before telling someone a job is finished, when a status update says "done" or "live", when an agent has gone quiet, or when deciding whether to merge. Do not use to re-review code quality in depth; use a code review or adversarial-verification for that.
old.expert-council: Review and improve an idea, document, design, plan, research argument, workflow, or code with five distinct expert critic perspectives, a focused debate, and a shared recommendation. Use when the user asks for Expert Council, five critics, multiple personalities reviewing something, a panel of experts, or a debate that produces suggestions and improvements. Also use when the user explicitly wants several perspectives to challenge and refine a proposal together. Do not activate for ordinary proofreading, a simple factual question, or routine implementation without a request for this review process.
old.job-brief: Turn a request into a job brief another agent can build from without guessing, and have the builder answer with a plan grounded in the actual code before it starts. Use when delegating coding work to an agent or subagent, writing a ticket or issue for a builder, packing work for a parallel worker, or when a builder is about to start without a clear definition of done. Do not use for one-line fixes you will do yourself.
old.retrieval-routing-patterns: Design or review RAG, search, tool/skill discovery and specialist routing so retrieval stays safe and useful. Use when working on retrieval pipelines, query rewriting or expansion, hybrid search, reranking, progressive tool disclosure, capability search, routing to specialists, or defending against prompt injection through retrieved content or tool descriptions.
old.runtime-pacing: Apply shared run-time awareness to non-trivial agent or multi-agent work so executors pace toward an optional soft latency target without weakening authority, required review, safety, verification, or evidence. Use when a run has elapsed-time or latency pressure, when helpers join an existing run, when an orchestrator asks to converge or finish efficiently, or when a packet says "Apply RUNTIME-PACING". Do not use it as a replacement for the host runtime, router, scheduler, lease system, heartbeat, hard timeout, or approval gates.
old.ui-adversarial-testing: Use when QA needs to actively try to break a changed web UI, explore edge cases around a pull request, or test user flows beyond the happy path with browser evidence.

new.adversarial-verification: Tries to prove a claim wrong before you trust it: hunts counterexamples, checks whether the checker itself could pass while the thing is broken, and gives a PASS / REPAIR / REJECT / NOT VERIFIED verdict. Use when someone says "verified", "proved", "safe", "fixed" or "beats the benchmark", or before a research, security or benchmark claim others will rely on. Not for routine code review.
new.check-the-work: Checks whether delegated work is really done by looking at git, CI and the running system instead of trusting the report. Use when an agent, subagent or teammate says "done", "fixed", "pushed", "CI green", "deployed" or "live", before you tell anyone it is finished, before merging, or when a worker has gone quiet. Not for in-depth code quality review.
new.expert-council: Puts an idea, plan, document or code in front of five critics (strategist, analyst, challenger, builder, audience advocate), recomputes its numbers, runs a short debate and ends with one recommendation. Use when asked for an expert council, a panel, several perspectives, or a debate on a proposal. Not for proofreading, simple facts or routine implementation.
new.job-brief: Writes a one-screen job brief another agent can build from without guessing (done-when, must-not-change, limits, tests, handback) and has the builder reply with a plan from the real code first. Use when delegating coding work to an agent or subagent, writing a ticket or issue for a builder, or when a builder is about to start without a clear definition of done. Not for one-line fixes you will do yourself.
new.retrieval-routing-patterns: A security-first checklist for RAG, search and tool routing: filter by permission before retrieval, treat retrieved text and tool descriptions as untrusted, bind approvals to exact arguments, and never invent answers on empty results. Use when building or reviewing RAG pipelines, search, reranking, tool or skill discovery, specialist routing, or prompt-injection defences in retrieved content.
new.runtime-pacing: Keeps agents on a shared run clock so they explore early, converge near a time target and stop at an honest checkpoint, without ever skipping tests, reviews, approvals or deadline gates. Use when a run has a time or latency target, a deadline or cutoff, helpers joining mid-run, or an instruction to "hurry", "converge" or "ship it fast". Not a replacement for the runtime's scheduler, timeouts or approval gates.
new.ui-adversarial-testing: Tries to break a changed web UI the way real people do (double-submit, Escape and refresh mid-flow, empty and huge input, slow networks, narrow screens) and reports each check as PASS, FAIL, SKIP or NOT RUN with evidence. Use when QA-ing a pull request or new feature, testing beyond the happy path, or when asked "can you test this" or "try to break it". Without a browser it marks checks NOT RUN instead of passing them.
